en: Sutta Nipāta 2.2 Āmagandhasutta “[Eating] millet,
wild greens, and cīnaka grain, ...”
Eating pāṭalī fruit, root fruit, and gavippha fruit—
obtained righteously and eating with mindfulness— they,
not desiring sensual pleasures, do not speak falsehood.
When one eats well-prepared and well-cooked food,
given by others, offered with devotion and of excellent quality— such as the rice of the finest grain— while partaking of it, [one experiences the fruit of that merit].
"Thus you eat raw flesh, Kassapa," so you say,
"raw flesh is not permitted for me," O kinsman of Brahmā.
While eating fine rice well-prepared with the meat of birds,
I ask you this matter, Kassapa:
“What kind of raw stench is yours?
“Killing living beings, slaughter, cutting, and binding;
theft, false speech, and deceitful fraud.”
Reciting spells and adultery—
this is the foul odor, not the eating of meat.
Those people here who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures,
Greedy for flavors, immersed in impurity,
holding nihilistic views, erratic and difficult to guide—
this is the foul stench, not indeed the eating of meat.
Those who are harsh and cruel, who backbite,
who betray friends, who are pitiless and arrogant,
who are stingy by nature and give nothing to anyone—
This is the scent of the impure, for it is not the scent of meat-eating:
anger, intoxication, rigidity, contentiousness,
deceit, envy, and the proliferation of talk.
Arrogance, excessive pride, and intimacy with the wicked—
this is the foul odor, not the eating of meat.
Those who are evil in conduct, debtors, murderers, and informers—
Those who engage in fraudulent speech and act as deceivers here,
these lowest of men who commit evil deeds—
this is the "raw-flesh stench," for it is not the eating of meat.
Those people here who are unrestrained toward living beings,
who take what belongs to others and are intent on harming them—
being immoral, greedy, harsh, and disrespectful—
This is the scent of peace, for it is not the food of meat.
Those who are greedy for these things, who are hostile and murderous,
and who are constantly engaged in such acts, go to darkness after death.
Beings fall headlong into hell;
this is the foul stench, not the eating of meat.
Abstaining from fish and meat is not fasting.
Neither nakedness, nor shaving the head, nor matted hair and dirt,
nor rough skins and antelope hides, nor the tending of the sacred fire,
nor even the many austerities practiced by those in the world who claim immortality— none of these purify a person who has not overcome doubt.
Sacrifices with mantras, oblations,
and seasonal rites do not purify a mortal who has not crossed over doubt.
One should wander with the sense-faculties guarded and their range well understood.
Established in the Dhamma, delighting in uprightness and gentleness,
having transcended attachments and abandoned all suffering,
the wise one is not defiled by what is seen or heard.
The Blessed One, who has reached the further shore of the mantras, repeatedly declared this meaning;
the Sage made it clear through various verses.
Free from the stench of raw flesh, unattached, and difficult to fathom—
having heard this well-spoken word of the Buddha,
which is free from the stench of raw flesh and dispels all suffering;
With a humble mind, he paid homage to the Tathāgata and right there expressed his desire for the going forth.
Thus ends the second discourse, the Āmagandha Sutta.
